claims.claim: A metaphor is a figure of speech that makes a comparison without pointing out a similarity with words such as 'like,' 'as,' or 'than'; it speaks of one thing as another.
Metaphors compare by selecting one aspect or a few aspects that things which are otherwise completely different share; this selective comparison is an essential part of rhetorical language.

The two parts of a metaphor are its tenor, the primary subject being described, and its vehicle, the secondary subject or image through which the primary subject is presented; this terminology is associated with I.A. Richards (The Philosophy of Rhetoric, 1936).
An extended metaphor is a single comparison sustained across multiple successive sentences or an entire passage, rather than confined to one clause.
A mixed metaphor leaps from one identification to a second inconsistent with the first, and the clash of images is often comic or confusing.
A dead metaphor is one in which the sense of the transferred image has become so familiar that it goes unnoticed, as in 'grasp a concept'; a live metaphor still makes its comparison felt.

Lakoff and Johnson (Metaphors We Live By, 1980) argued that metaphor is at bottom a conceptual matter: people think of one kind of thing in terms of another, through standing cross-domain mappings such as 'love is a journey' or 'argument is war'; this is a theory about thought and language, not a claim that every metaphor works the same way.

A simile is an explicit comparison built around 'like,' 'as,' or another explicit comparative construction, whereas a metaphor is the implicit form that states an identification; the distinction is brief in this lesson because simile has its own topic.

Analogy is comparison based on a real or supposed likeness or parallel relationship, and it is often spelled out at length; metaphor can be understood as a compact form of comparison that leaves the likeness implicit.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a dead (conventionalized) metaphor should still be called a metaphor at all, since its image is no longer noticed.
positions: Some definitions treat only live, noticeable comparisons as metaphors and call worn-out ones literal language or cliches.
Other treatments use 'dead metaphor' for exactly those unnoticed transferred images, and note that some authors distinguish dead metaphors from cliches while others use the terms interchangeably.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson defines dead metaphor as a metaphor whose transferred image goes unnoticed and explicitly notes the term describes noticeability, not quality; it avoids claiming a single authoritative boundary.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The scope of conceptual metaphor theory: whether metaphors like 'argument is war' actually shape thought or merely reflect it.
positions: Lakoff and Johnson maintain that metaphor is fundamentally conceptual and pervasive in everyday thinking.
Philosophers of language offer competing accounts of metaphor's meaning and do not all accept the strong conceptualist claim.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents conceptual metaphor as an attributed theory (Lakoff and Johnson, 1980) and frames it as a framework for noticing patterns in language, not as a settled fact or a rule for interpreting individual metaphors.
